# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** October 18, 2026
**Re:** Halvorsen Industrial Holdings LLC / Acquisition of Corbel Fluidics, Inc.: Buyer-side issues review of transaction documents
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the four documents in the folder:

- **SPA:** the Stock Purchase Agreement dated September 21, 2026, with its Disclosure Schedule.
- **Supply Agreement:** the Corbel–Vantrell Master Supply Agreement.
- **Side Letter:** the Seller indemnity side letter.
- **Escrow Agreement:** the form of escrow agreement.

Five substantive issues leave Halvorsen exposed. They are listed below with the most significant first.

| # | Issue | Location | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vantrell's change-of-control consent and termination right are not addressed in the SPA | Supply Agreement §14.2; SPA §4.4, Sched. 4.4, §§6.3, 7.2(c) | **Critical** |
| 2 | Side Letter narrows Fundamental Representations, so Capitalization and Taxes become capped | Side Letter §2; SPA §§1.1, 9.5, 11.11 | **Critical** |
| 3 | Company's extension option at locked pricing lapsed before signing | Supply Agreement §§3.1, 3.2 | **High** (valuation) |
| 4 | Side Letter moves indemnity disputes to Delaware law and the Court of Chancery | Side Letter §6; SPA §§11.8, 11.9, 11.11 | **High** |
| 5 | Vantrell may assign the sole-source contract freely, including to a competitor | Supply Agreement §16.1 | **Medium–High** |

Key deal economics for reference:

- **Purchase Price:** $84,500,000 (SPA §2.1).
- **Escrow Amount:** $8,450,000 (SPA §2.5).
- **Deductible:** $633,750 (SPA §9.5(a)).
- **General indemnity Cap:** **10% of the Purchase Price, i.e., $8,450,000** (SPA §9.5(a)). The Cap equals the escrow.

**Order of precedence.** SPA §11.11 ranks the Transaction Documents as follows: **first the Side Letter, then the SPA, then the Escrow Agreement.** The Side Letter therefore controls over the SPA wherever they conflict. That clause is what turns Issues 2 and 4 from drafting inconsistencies into real changes to the deal.

Points needing a client call are collected in Section 3. Gaps and ambiguities in the folder are listed in Section 4.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Vantrell change-of-control consent not addressed (Critical)

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §14.2.
- SPA §4.4 and Disclosure Schedule 4.4 ("None").
- SPA §6.3 and §7.2(c).
- SPA §4.10 and Schedule 4.10 (the Supply Agreement is listed as a Material Contract and is the sole-source supply contract).

**What the documents say:**
- **The trigger.** Supply Agreement §14.2 provides that "[a]ny change in the direct or indirect ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting stock of Customer, whether by sale or transfer of stock … shall be deemed an assignment of this Agreement by Customer and shall require the prior written consent of Supplier."
- **The consequence.** If the change occurs without that consent, Vantrell may terminate on 30 days' written notice.
- **This deal triggers it.** Halvorsen's purchase of 100% of the Shares falls squarely within §14.2.
- **The SPA does not deal with it.**
  - In §4.4, Seller represents that no consent is required under any Material Contract.
  - Schedule 4.4 reads "None."
  - The Seller covenant to seek consents (§6.3) is limited to consents listed on Schedule 4.4.
  - The closing condition (§7.2(c)) is also limited to consents listed on Schedule 4.4.
- **Result.** Nothing obliges Seller to obtain Vantrell's consent, and nothing conditions Closing on it.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**
- **Supply risk.** Vantrell is Corbel's sole-source resin supplier under a 100% requirements arrangement (Supply Agreement §2.2). Halvorsen could close and then receive a 30-day termination notice, leaving the business without its critical input. Vantrell could also use the termination right as leverage to reprice.
- **Weak remedy.** Halvorsen's only remedy would be an indemnity claim for breach of §4.4, which is a general representation. That claim would be:
  - subject to the $633,750 Deductible;
  - subject to the $8,450,000 Cap; and
  - limited to an 18-month survival period.
- **Inadequate measure of loss.** The Cap would very likely be inadequate against loss of the business's sole-source supply.
- **Exclusive remedy.** Article IX is the exclusive post-Closing remedy (§9.8).

**Leverage:**
- §4.4 is inaccurate today.
- §7.2(a) requires the representations to be true in all material respects at Closing.
- §8.1(b) gives Halvorsen a termination right for uncured breach.
- Seller should therefore have every incentive to fix this pre-Closing.

**Recommendation:**
1. Require Seller to correct Schedule 4.4 to list the Vantrell consent under Supply Agreement §14.2.
2. Expressly make receipt of that consent a Buyer closing condition.
3. Require that the consent be unconditional and contain a waiver of the §14.2 termination right for this transaction.

Proposed SPA amendment:

> **Schedule 4.4, item 1:** "Prior written consent of Vantrell Polymer Corp. under Section 14.2 of the Supply Agreement to the change in ownership of the Company contemplated by this Agreement."
>
> **New Section 7.2(g):** "Buyer shall have received a written consent of Vantrell Polymer Corp., in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, (i) consenting under Section 14.2 of the Supply Agreement to the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, (ii) irrevocably waiving any right to terminate, modify or reprice the Supply Agreement by reason of such transactions, and (iii) containing no other amendment to the Supply Agreement not approved in writing by Buyer."
>
> **Section 6.3 (revised):** "…use reasonable best efforts to obtain all consents from the third parties described on Schedule 4.4, including the Vantrell consent described in Section 7.2(g), at Seller's sole cost; provided that neither Seller nor the Company shall agree to any payment, concession or amendment in connection therewith without Buyer's prior written consent."

**Fallback:** If Seller resists the closing condition, seek a stand-alone special indemnity. It should cover all Losses arising from any termination or repricing of the Supply Agreement attributable to the change of control. It should sit outside the Deductible and Cap, and be backed by a separate escrow holdback.

The consent negotiation is also the natural place to address Issues 3 and 5.

---

### Issue 2: Side Letter narrows Fundamental Representations, so Capitalization and Taxes become capped (Critical)

**Where:**
- Side Letter §2.
- SPA §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representations").
- SPA §§7.2(a), 9.1, 9.5(a)–(b) and 11.11.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA definition.** SPA §1.1 defines Fundamental Representations as §§4.1, 4.2, **4.3 (Capitalization) and 4.12 (Taxes)**.
- **SPA carve-out.** Under §9.5(b), the Deductible and the 10% Cap do not apply to breaches of Fundamental Representations. Under §9.1, Fundamental Representations survive until 60 days after the statute of limitations.
- **Side Letter redefinition.** Side Letter §2 provides that "[f]or all purposes of the Purchase Agreement, including Sections 7.2(a), 9.1 and 9.5(b) thereof, 'Fundamental Representations' means **solely Sections 4.1 and 4.2**."
- **Precedence.** SPA §11.11 gives the Side Letter priority over the SPA. The Side Letter's narrower definition therefore governs.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:** Under the documents as drafted, the §4.3 Capitalization and §4.12 Taxes representations are no longer uncapped. In practice:

- **Capitalization (§4.3).** This covers title to the Shares, no Encumbrances, no options or warrants, and no subsidiaries. Breaches would now be:
  - subject to the $633,750 Deductible;
  - subject to the **$8,450,000 Cap**; and
  - limited to an **18-month** survival period.

  A title or capitalization defect goes to whether Halvorsen received what it paid $84.5 million for. A recovery limited to 10% of the price is not appropriate for that risk.
- **Taxes (§4.12).** The same Deductible, Cap and 18-month survival now apply. Tax audits commonly arise well after 18 months.
  - *Partial mitigation:* the separate pre-Closing Tax indemnity in SPA §9.2(c) remains outside the Cap under §9.5(b), and the Side Letter does not touch it.
  - *Remaining gaps:* §4.12 also covers matters §9.2(c) may not reach cleanly, such as return accuracy, withholding, and audit and waiver status. In addition, the survival period for §9.2(c) claims is not clearly stated (see Section 4).
- **Closing condition.** The §7.2(a) standard for Capitalization and Taxes drops from "true and correct in all respects" to "in all material respects."

**Recommendation:** Strike Side Letter §2 in its entirety. Alternatively, conform it to SPA §1.1. In either case, Seller should confirm in writing that nothing in the Side Letter limits Article IX protection.

Proposed Side Letter amendment:

> "Section 2 of this Letter Agreement is deleted in its entirety. For the avoidance of doubt, 'Fundamental Representations' has the meaning given in Section 1.1 of the Purchase Agreement, being Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 (Capitalization) and 4.12 (Taxes) thereof."

I also recommend narrowing SPA §11.11 so the Side Letter cannot silently override SPA risk allocation in the future:

> "…first, the Side Letter, solely with respect to the matters expressly addressed in Sections 3 and 4 thereof; second, this Agreement; …"

---

### Issue 3: Company's extension option at locked pricing lapsed before signing (High, valuation)

**Where:** Supply Agreement §§3.1, 3.2, 5.3 and Schedule B, Part 2.

**What the documents say:**
- **Initial Term.** It ends **December 31, 2026** (§3.1).
- **Option.** Under §3.2, Corbel may extend for 36 months at the **Extension Pricing**. That pricing is fixed for the full Extension Term and is not subject to the quarterly raw-material adjustment (§5.3; Schedule B, Part 2).
- **Notice deadline.** Exercise requires written notice "not less than one hundred twenty (120) days before the end of the Initial Term." Absent timely notice, the agreement "expires at the end of the Initial Term."
- **The deadline has passed.** 120 days before December 31, 2026 is on or about **September 2, 2026**. The SPA was signed **September 21, 2026**, nineteen days later.
- **No exercise shown.** Nothing in the folder shows the option was exercised.

**Conclusion:** Unless Seller can produce a timely notice, the extension right and the Extension Pricing have been lost, and the Supply Agreement expires on December 31, 2026.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**
- **Imminent expiry.** Corbel's sole-source supply contract would expire roughly ten weeks from today, about two weeks after the SPA's December 15, 2026 outside date (§8.1(d)).
- **Weaker negotiating position.** Corbel would have to renegotiate from a weak position with a supplier that also holds the change-of-control consent right (Issue 1).
- **Pricing loss.** Corbel loses three years of locked, non-indexed pricing.
- **Valuation and disclosure.** This is presumably reflected in neither the Purchase Price nor the Disclosure Schedule. Halvorsen should consider whether a claim exists under §4.7 (Absence of Certain Changes) or §4.10(b). Any such claim would be capped, and the facts may not amount to a "breach" of those representations as drafted.

**Recommendation:**
1. **Confirm the facts first** (see Section 3). Ask Seller to confirm in writing whether any extension notice was delivered and, if so, to produce it.
2. **If the option lapsed,** pursue one or more of the following:
   - **(a) Renegotiation as a closing condition.** A pre-Closing renewal or extension with Vantrell, negotiated alongside the §14.2 consent, on terms acceptable to Halvorsen. It should run at least 36 months at pricing no worse than Extension Pricing. Under SPA §6.1(c), Seller cannot cause Corbel to amend the Supply Agreement without Halvorsen's consent, which gives Halvorsen control over those terms.
   - **(b) Price adjustment.** A reduction reflecting the modelled cost differential over the expected supply period.
   - **(c) Special indemnity.** An uncapped indemnity for incremental resin costs above Extension Pricing for 36 months, secured by an additional holdback.

Illustrative closing condition:

> "**Section 7.2(h):** The Company and Vantrell Polymer Corp. shall have entered into a written amendment to the Supply Agreement, in form and substance satisfactory to Buyer, extending the Term through at least December 31, 2029 at prices not exceeding the Extension Pricing set forth in Part 2 of Schedule B thereto."

---

### Issue 4: Side Letter moves indemnity disputes to Delaware law and the Court of Chancery (High)

**Where:** Side Letter §6.1–6.2; SPA §§11.8, 11.9 and 11.11; Escrow Agreement §§8.1–8.2.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA.** §11.8 selects **New York law** for all claims "arising out of or related to this Agreement." §11.9 requires exclusive jurisdiction in the state or federal courts in **New York County** for disputes under the SPA *and the other Transaction Documents*.
- **Side Letter.** §6 provides that "all claims, disputes and causes of action arising out of or relating to indemnification under the Purchase Agreement" are governed by the **laws of the State of Delaware**. Such suits must be brought exclusively in the **Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware**.
- **Precedence.** Because §11.11 gives the Side Letter priority, Article IX indemnity claims would go to Delaware under Delaware law.
- **Everything else stays in New York.** This includes other SPA claims, specific performance, Fraud claims outside the indemnity framework, and Escrow Agreement disputes (Escrow Agreement §§8.1–8.2).

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**
- **Split forum and law.** A single dispute over a misrepresentation could fracture across two courts and two bodies of law. Typical examples are an indemnity claim combined with a Fraud claim or an escrow release fight. That creates cost, delay and a risk of inconsistent rulings.
- **Uncertain substantive rules.** Fraud is defined by reference to New York law (§1.1). Questions such as sandbagging, reliance and the effect of the exclusive-remedy clause may be resolved differently in Delaware than under the New York law Halvorsen negotiated.
- **Lost bargain.** It undercuts the New York forum Halvorsen bargained for.
- **Escrow mechanics.** The Escrow Agreement's Final Order mechanism (§4.3) accepts any court of competent jurisdiction, so a Delaware judgment would still release funds. However, any interpleader under Escrow Agreement §6.6 would proceed in New York.

**Recommendation:** Conform Side Letter §6 to the SPA.

> "**6.1** This Letter Agreement, and all claims or causes of action based upon, arising out of or related to this Letter Agreement or indemnification under the Purchase Agreement, shall be governed by the internal Laws of the State of New York, consistent with Section 11.8 of the Purchase Agreement.
>
> **6.2** Section 11.9 (Submission to Jurisdiction) of the Purchase Agreement applies to this Letter Agreement *mutatis mutandis*, and any suit, action or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Letter Agreement or indemnification under the Purchase Agreement shall be instituted exclusively in the state or federal courts located in New York County, New York."

The §11.11 narrowing proposed under Issue 2 would also prevent this kind of override.

---

### Issue 5: Vantrell may assign the sole-source contract freely, including to a competitor (Medium–High)

**Where:** Supply Agreement §16.1.

**What the document says:** §16.1 is one-sided.
- **Corbel** may not assign without Vantrell's prior written consent. The change-of-control deemed-assignment in §14.2 reinforces this.
- **Vantrell** "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, to any Person **without the consent of Customer**." This expressly includes assignment in connection with a merger or a sale of all or any part of Vantrell's resin business.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**
- **Competitor control of supply.** Vantrell could transfer Corbel's sole-source supply contract to a Halvorsen competitor, or to a financially weaker or less capable party.
- **Partial assignments.** "In whole or in part" permits partial assignments, for example of particular product grades. That could fragment supply, quality accountability and the §2.3 capacity commitments.
- **Information exposure.** An assignee would receive Corbel's monthly 12-month Forecasts, pricing and Specifications. These are Confidential Information under §10.1, but the assignee would be entitled to use them under the contract.
- **No exit.** The 100% requirements obligation (§2.2) means Corbel has no contractual exit if an undesirable assignee takes over.

**Recommendation:** Seek a mutual consent requirement with a competitor carve-out. The most practical route is to negotiate it with Vantrell in the same instrument as the §14.2 consent and the renewal (Issues 1 and 3).

Proposed replacement §16.1, second sentence:

> "Supplier may not assign or otherwise transfer this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of Customer (not to be unreasonably withheld), except that Supplier may assign this Agreement in its entirety, without consent but upon prior written notice, to a successor to all or substantially all of Supplier's resin business that (a) assumes all of Supplier's obligations in writing, (b) is not a Competitor of Customer or any of its Affiliates, and (c) has the manufacturing capability and quality certifications required by Sections 2.3 and 8.1. 'Competitor' means any Person (or Affiliate of a Person) engaged in the design or manufacture of fluid-handling components. Customer may terminate this Agreement on ninety (90) days' notice following any assignment by Supplier to which Customer has not consented."

**Fallback:** If Vantrell will not amend, Halvorsen should at least price this risk into its supply planning. It should also consider a dual-sourcing qualification program after Closing.

---

## 3. Points to raise with the client before we respond

1. **Vantrell relationship and approach (Issues 1, 3 and 5).** We need to confirm with the client:
   - whether Halvorsen is willing to condition Closing on the Vantrell consent and a renewal;
   - whether Halvorsen or its personnel have any existing relationship with Vantrell; and
   - who should make the approach (Seller/Company or jointly), and when.

   A combined consent, renewal and assignment amendment is likely the most efficient route, but it depends on the client's appetite and the outside date.
2. **Extension option status (Issue 3).** Does the client know, from diligence, whether Corbel sent an extension notice before September 2, 2026? Has the client's valuation model assumed Extension Pricing through 2029? The answer determines whether we ask for a price adjustment, a special indemnity or a renewal condition, and how large any of those should be.
3. **How the Side Letter terms arose (Issues 2 and 4).** Did the client, or anyone acting for it, knowingly agree to the narrowed Fundamental Representations and the Delaware forum as a negotiated trade? We should know this before characterizing these terms to Seller as errors or demanding they be struck.
4. **Remedies and timing.** The deal is signed, so each fix requires Seller's agreement (SPA §11.6). The client should decide how hard to press, given:
   - Halvorsen's leverage under §§4.4, 7.2(a) and 8.1(b); and
   - the December 15, 2026 outside date.

   The client should also decide whether to consider extending the outside date to allow the Vantrell negotiation.
5. **Risk tolerance on the Cap.** If Seller refuses to restore Capitalization and Taxes as Fundamental Representations, would the client accept alternatives such as R&W insurance, a larger escrow, or longer survival for those representations?

---

## 4. Gaps and points of uncertainty in the folder

- **Execution status.** The SPA and Side Letter are dated September 21, 2026, but the signature blocks in the folder copies are blank. I have assumed both are signed and binding, since the SPA recites signing and the instruction refers to a signed agreement. Please confirm. If they are still unsigned drafts, all of the above can be fixed by mark-up rather than amendment.
- **Supply Agreement amendments.** The SPA defines the Supply Agreement "as amended through the date of this Agreement," and Schedule 4.10 refers to "all amendments thereto." The folder contains only the original December 15, 2021 agreement. We should obtain any amendments, waivers or side arrangements. Any of these could have extended the term, varied §14.2 or §16.1, or recorded an option exercise.
- **Evidence of option exercise.** The folder contains no correspondence between Corbel and Vantrell. My conclusion on Issue 3 is that the option lapsed, but it rests on the absence of any notice in the folder.
- **Escrow Agreement.** This is a form only. The date, Exhibit B representatives and investment designation are blank. It is consistent with the SPA on amount ($8,450,000), the 18-month release and New York law and forum, and I found no substantive issue in it beyond the forum interaction noted in Issue 4. Note that release under Escrow Agreement §4.4 depends on a Joint Written Instruction, which ties to Side Letter §4.
- **Survival of the §9.2(c) Tax indemnity.** SPA §9.1 sets survival for representations and covenants but does not expressly address the stand-alone pre-Closing Tax indemnity in §9.2(c). Following the Side Letter's narrowing of §4.12, this indemnity is Halvorsen's main uncapped tax protection. We should seek express survival until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations.
- **Other Disclosure Schedule references.** Target working capital ($6,200,000) and the other Material Contracts listed (the First Meridian credit facility, the Ostrander distribution agreement and the Parkway lease) are not in the folder. I have not reviewed whether those contracts contain their own change-of-control or anti-assignment provisions. Given the pattern in the Supply Agreement, they should be checked before we rely on Schedule 4.4 being otherwise complete.

Please let me know if you would like me to turn these recommendations into a consolidated amendment and Side Letter mark-up for circulation to Seller's counsel.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** October 18, 2026
**Re:** Halvorsen Industrial Holdings LLC / Acquisition of Corbel Fluidics, Inc.: Buyer-side issues in the current transaction documents

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the four documents in the folder:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated September 21, 2026 and its Disclosure Schedule (the "SPA");
- the Corbel–Vantrell Master Supply Agreement dated December 15, 2021 (the "Supply Agreement");
- the Seller indemnity side letter dated September 21, 2026 (the "Side Letter"); and
- the form Escrow Agreement with Granite Ledger Trust Company.

Four substantive issues leave Halvorsen exposed. In order of significance:

1. **The Side Letter strips Capitalization and Taxes out of the uncapped Fundamental Representations.** Because SPA Section 11.11 gives the Side Letter precedence, breaches of those representations are now subject to the 10% cap ($8,450,000).
2. **Vantrell's change-of-control consent under Supply Agreement Section 14.2 is triggered but not addressed.** The SPA neither discloses it nor makes it a closing condition. Vantrell can terminate the sole-source contract on 30 days' notice after Closing.
3. **The Company's extension option at locked Extension Pricing lapsed on September 2, 2026,** nineteen days before signing. The Supply Agreement now expires December 31, 2026.
4. **Vantrell may assign the Supply Agreement freely** under Section 16.1, including to a Halvorsen competitor, while the Company cannot assign without Vantrell's consent.

Issues 2 through 4 all concern the Company's single most important commercial relationship. They should be approached together with Vantrell. Points requiring a client call are collected in Section 3. Gaps in the folder are listed in Section 4.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Side Letter narrows the Fundamental Representations and moves Capitalization and Taxes under the cap

**Where:**
- Side Letter, Section 2
- SPA Sections 1.1 ("Fundamental Representations"), 9.5(a)–(b), 9.1, 7.2(a) and 11.11

**What the documents say:**
- **The SPA.** Section 1.1 defines Fundamental Representations as Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 (Capitalization) and 4.12 (Taxes). Under Section 9.5(a), Seller's liability for representation breaches is subject to a $633,750 Deductible and a Cap of 10% of the Purchase Price, which is $8,450,000 on the $84,500,000 price. Section 9.5(b) carves Fraud and Fundamental Representation breaches out of both limits.
- **The Side Letter.** Section 2 provides that "[f]or all purposes of the Purchase Agreement, including Sections 7.2(a), 9.1 and 9.5(b) thereof," Fundamental Representations means "solely Sections 4.1 and 4.2."
- **Precedence.** SPA Section 11.11 sets the order of precedence among the Transaction Documents as: first, the Side Letter; second, the SPA; third, the Escrow Agreement. The Side Letter therefore controls, and Side Letter Section 7.1 confirms that the SPA is modified to that extent.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**

- **Capitalization (4.3) is now capped.** This representation covers title to the Shares, absence of Encumbrances, and absence of options or warrants. It goes to whether Halvorsen actually receives what it is paying $84.5 million for. Under the current documents, a title or capitalization defect is recoverable only above the $633,750 Deductible and only up to $8,450,000.
- **Taxes (4.12) is now capped.** Section 4.12 representation claims are now subject to the Deductible and Cap. The stand-alone pre-Closing tax indemnity in Section 9.2(c) remains uncapped under Section 9.5(b), which partly mitigates this. However:
  - Section 9.2(c) covers only "Taxes of the Company" for pre-Closing periods.
  - It does not reach Losses arising from other inaccuracies in 4.12, such as false statements that no audits are pending or that no statute-of-limitations waivers are in effect.
  - We should not rely on 9.2(c) as a full substitute.
- **Survival is shortened.** Under Section 9.1, Capitalization and Taxes now survive only 18 months, rather than until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations. Tax exposure in particular often surfaces well after 18 months.
- **The bring-down standard is weakened.** Under Section 7.2(a), Capitalization and Taxes now need to be true only "in all material respects" at Closing, rather than "in all respects."
- **The narrowing sits outside the main agreement.** A reader of the SPA alone would conclude these representations are uncapped. That makes this easy to miss later.

**Recommendation:**

Strike Side Letter Section 2 in its entirety. If Seller insists on keeping the provision, conform it to the SPA:

> "2. Fundamental Representations. For all purposes of the Purchase Agreement, 'Fundamental Representations' has the meaning given in Section 1.1 of the Purchase Agreement, being Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 (Capitalization) and 4.12 (Taxes) thereof. Nothing in this Letter Agreement limits, narrows or otherwise modifies that definition or Sections 7.2(a), 9.1 or 9.5(b) of the Purchase Agreement."

Separately, we should consider amending SPA Section 11.11 so that the Side Letter cannot override Article IX protections in Buyer's favor:

> "…provided, however, that no provision of the Side Letter shall be construed to limit or reduce any right or remedy of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX of this Agreement unless such provision expressly refers to this proviso."

---

### Issue 2: Vantrell change-of-control consent is triggered but not addressed in the SPA

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement, Section 14.2
- SPA Sections 4.4, 6.3 and 7.2(c), and Disclosure Schedule 4.4

**What the documents say:**

- **Supply Agreement Section 14.2.** Any change in the "direct or indirect ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting stock of Customer," including by sale of stock, is deemed an assignment by Customer and requires "the prior written consent of Supplier." If the change occurs without that consent, Vantrell may terminate on 30 days' written notice.
  - The sale of 100% of Corbel's Shares to Halvorsen squarely triggers this provision.
- **SPA Section 4.4.** Seller represents that the transaction does not require the consent of any Person under, or give rise to any right of termination under, any Material Contract, except as set forth on Schedule 4.4.
  - Schedule 4.4 reads "None."
  - The Supply Agreement is itself listed on Schedule 4.10 as a Material Contract, and Section 4.10(a)(ii) captures sole-source supply contracts.
- **SPA Sections 6.3 and 7.2(c).** Seller's covenant to seek consents (6.3) and the Buyer closing condition on consents (7.2(c)) extend only to items listed on Schedule 4.4. Nothing in the folder obtains Vantrell's consent or makes it a condition to Closing.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**

- **The supply relationship is critical.** Vantrell is the Company's sole-source resin supplier under a 100% requirements contract (Supply Agreement Section 2.2).
- **The termination risk is real.** If Halvorsen closes without consent, Vantrell can terminate on 30 days' notice. It could also use that threat to reprice.
- **The SPA gives Halvorsen no walk right.** As drafted, Halvorsen has no right to refuse to close because the consent has not been obtained. There is an arguable route through the Section 7.2(a) bring-down, because Section 4.4 is inaccurate. That route is indirect, and it invites dispute over materiality.
- **Post-Closing recourse is weak.** After Closing, Halvorsen's remedy would be an indemnity claim for breach of Section 4.4. That is a general representation, so the claim would sit under the $633,750 Deductible and the $8,450,000 Cap. Losing the sole-source supply could easily cost more than that.

**Recommendation:**

1. Require Seller to correct Schedule 4.4 so that it lists the Vantrell consent under Supply Agreement Section 14.2.
2. Add an express closing condition:

   > "7.2(g) The Company shall have received the written consent of Vantrell Polymer Corp. under Section 14.2 of the Supply Agreement to the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, which consent shall (i) be unconditional, (ii) waive any right of Supplier to terminate the Supply Agreement by reason of such transactions, and (iii) not be accompanied by any amendment to pricing or other material terms of the Supply Agreement not approved in writing by Buyer, and a copy thereof shall have been delivered to Buyer."

3. Strengthen SPA Section 6.3 for the Vantrell consent from "commercially reasonable efforts" to "reasonable best efforts." Give Buyer the right to participate in all communications with Vantrell.
4. As a fallback if Seller resists a condition, add a special indemnity outside the Cap and Deductible for Losses arising from any termination of, or adverse amendment to, the Supply Agreement resulting from the change of control.

Issues 3 and 4 below should be negotiated in the same conversation with Vantrell.

---

### Issue 3: The Company's extension option at Extension Pricing lapsed before signing

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement, Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 5.3, and Schedule B, Part 2

**What the documents say:**

- **Term.** Section 3.1 sets the Initial Term to end December 31, 2026.
- **Extension option.** Section 3.2 gives Customer a single 36-month extension at the "Extension Pricing." The Extension Pricing is fixed for the full Extension Term and is not subject to the quarterly raw-material adjustment (Section 5.3; Schedule B, Part 2).
- **Notice deadline.** The option must be exercised by written notice delivered "not less than one hundred twenty (120) days before the end of the Initial Term."
  - Counting back 120 days from December 31, 2026 gives a deadline of **September 2, 2026**.
- **Consequence of missing the deadline.** If notice is not delivered within that period, the agreement "expires at the end of the Initial Term."
- **Timing against the SPA.** The SPA was signed September 21, 2026, nineteen days after the deadline. Nothing in the folder shows that notice was given.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**

- **The extension right is lost.** Unless notice was in fact delivered by September 2, the Company has lost both the extension right and the fixed Extension Pricing.
- **The contract will expire within weeks of Closing.** The Supply Agreement expires December 31, 2026, about two weeks after the SPA's December 15, 2026 outside date in Section 8.1(d).
- **Halvorsen would close into a renegotiation with weak leverage.** Corbel has no alternative qualified source. Vantrell will know the Company has no contractual right to continued supply or locked pricing.
- **Valuation is likely affected.** The Purchase Price was presumably modeled on continued supply at known pricing. We should confirm this with the client.
- **The SPA does not reflect the lapse.** There is no disclosure against Sections 4.7 or 4.10. The Section 4.10(b) representation that each Material Contract is "in full force and effect" is technically true today, but it gives no protection against the contract running out.

**Recommendation:**

1. Ask Seller immediately for written confirmation of whether an extension notice was delivered, with a copy and proof of delivery. If one exists, request its inclusion in the data room and a representation to that effect.
2. If the option was not exercised, which we should assume until shown otherwise, pursue one or more of the following:
   - **(a) Pre-closing renegotiation as a closing condition.** Require a written extension or amendment with Vantrell, on terms reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, as a condition to Closing. Ideally obtain it in the same instrument as the Section 14.2 consent:

     > "7.2(h) The Company and Vantrell Polymer Corp. shall have entered into a written amendment to the Supply Agreement, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, extending the term thereof through not earlier than December 31, 2029 at prices not exceeding the Extension Pricing set forth in Part 2 of Schedule B thereto."

   - **(b) Purchase Price adjustment.** Seek a reduction reflecting the loss of locked pricing and supply certainty.
   - **(c) Special indemnity.** Add an indemnity, outside the Cap and Deductible, for incremental resin costs above Extension Pricing over a defined period (for example, 36 months), and for Losses from any supply interruption following expiry.

3. Add specific disclosure and a representation addressing the expiry of the Supply Agreement and the status of the Section 3.2 option.

### Issue 4: Vantrell may assign the Supply Agreement without the Company's consent

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement, Section 16.1 (read with Section 4.2 and Section 10)

**What the document says:**

Section 16.1 is one-sided:

- The Company, as Customer, may not assign without Vantrell's prior written consent.
- Vantrell "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Customer." This expressly includes assignment in connection with a merger or a sale of all or part of its resin business.

**Why it matters to Halvorsen:**

- **The supply contract could land with a competitor.** Vantrell could transfer the sole-source contract, or part of it, to a Halvorsen competitor or an otherwise unsuitable counterparty.
- **That assignee would receive sensitive information.** It would get Corbel's monthly 12-month Forecasts, pricing and Specifications (Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 10.1). It would also control Corbel's critical input.
- **Partial assignment creates operational risk.** The "in whole or in part" language allows Vantrell to split the product lines between assignees, which could fragment supply and quality accountability.
- **The issue is most acute post-acquisition.** Corbel will sit inside Halvorsen's group, and competitively sensitive volume data will be visible to whoever holds the contract.

**Recommendation:**

Negotiate a mutual consent requirement with a competitor carve-out. Do this as part of the Vantrell consent and extension discussions under Issues 2 and 3, because those discussions are where we have leverage. Proposed replacement for the second sentence of Section 16.1:

> "Supplier may not assign or otherwise transfer this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of Customer (not to be unreasonably withheld), except that Supplier may assign this Agreement in its entirety, without such consent, to a successor to all or substantially all of Supplier's resin business that (a) assumes in writing all of Supplier's obligations hereunder and (b) is not a competitor of Customer or any of its Affiliates; provided that Customer may withhold consent in its sole discretion to any assignment to a competitor of Customer or any of its Affiliates. Supplier shall give Customer not less than ninety (90) days' prior written notice of any proposed assignment."

If Vantrell will not agree to a consent right, a fallback is for Customer to have a termination right without penalty, including relief from the Section 2.4 minimum-volume shortfall payment, upon any assignment to a competitor. That should be paired with protective use restrictions on Forecasts and Confidential Information held by any assignee.

On the SPA side, consider a representation that Seller has no knowledge of any pending or proposed sale of Vantrell's resin business or assignment of the Supply Agreement.
